title: Tamsin and the Summer
premise: Ansel Sandoval, a wedding planner who quietly stopped believing in love after a betrayal eleven years ago, returns to the island town of Marrow Bay to stage one last society wedding and finds an undelivered letter postmarked the summer they left—written by Tamsin Vey, the person they loved and abandoned without explanation. As Ansel plans a wedding built on someone else's borrowed happiness, they must track down Tamsin, now running the ferry service and fighting a developer's claim on her family's dock, and finally speak the sentence rehearsed for a decade. The climax comes at the last ferry of the season, when Ansel chooses truth over safety, confessing that they left because staying meant admitting they were loved; Tamsin, having spent years learning to belong to herself first, lets them aboard anyway. The book ends not with a wedding but with a crossing: two people choosing each other in daylight, on open water.
about_author: Gideon Halloran is the pen name of a former small-town newspaper reporter who covered harbor disputes and county fairs before turning to fiction. They write romances about people who mistake self-protection for personality, and live within sight of a ferry terminal they refuse to take for granted.

chapters.title: The Muscle That Learns
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. In Boston, Ansel directs a flawless wedding while privately reciting their creed: the heart is trainable, containable. A phone call from Marrow Bay—a favor owed, one last job—cracks the routine. Emotional beat: control presented as peace, already fraying at the edges.

chapters.title: Postmarked Eleven Years Ago
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. Arriving on the island, Ansel collects mail held at the old guesthouse and finds a letter addressed to them, postmarked the summer they vanished. They can't bring themselves to open it. Beat: dread disguised as curiosity; the past made physical.

chapters.title: The Wedding of Borrowed Weather
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. Ansel meets clients Priya and June, whose wedding is being bankrolled by June's family—and quietly entangled with the developer buying up the waterfront. Ansel takes the job as cover. Beat: complicity; beauty built on someone else's terms.

chapters.title: Ferry Number Seven
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Tamsin runs the last independent ferry line, fighting an eminent-domain claim on her family dock. She spots Ansel at the terminal and says nothing, only charges them double out of spite. Beat: old wound, new armor.

chapters.title: What the Letter Said
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. Alone, Ansel finally opens the letter: eleven years ago, Tamsin wrote that she was ready—that she'd chosen Ansel—and asked them to say yes or no plainly. Ansel never answered. Beat: shame arriving late, fully grown.

chapters.title: Negotiations at the Dock
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Ansel needs ferry access for wedding guests; Tamsin needs a witness statement about the dock's history—one Ansel is uniquely positioned to give. They strike a wary bargain. Beat: transactional intimacy, both pretending it's just business.

chapters.title: Inventory of Small Mercies
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Preparing the boat for the season's end, Tamsin catalogs what the dock means: her father's tools, her mother's handwriting on the fuel log. She admits to herself she never stopped waiting, and hates it. Beat: grief for time spent holding still.

chapters.title: Rehearsal Dinner, Unrehearsed
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. A tasting event goes sideways when the developer, Halloran Group's local man, uses it to court islanders. Ansel watches June flinch under her family's expectations and recognizes the performance. Beat: Ansel's cynicism curdling into something like conscience.

chapters.title: The Sentence, First Draft
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. Late at night on the empty beach, Ansel tries to say the rehearsed sentence aloud—I left because you were ready and I wasn't—and fails. They write it instead, then burn the page. Beat: rehearsal as avoidance; words easier burned than spoken.

chapters.title: Storm Warning
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. A gale damages the dock; the developer offers a rescue loan with strings attached. Tamsin refuses on principle and immediately regrets the arithmetic. Beat: pride versus survival; justice outside the law starts costing real money.

chapters.title: Witness
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. Ansel digs into old records and finds proof the dock predates every claim against it—their own family's name in the ledger. Giving it to Tamsin means exposing why their family really left. Beat: the choice between safety and testimony.

chapters.title: Midsummer Fair
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. At the island fair, Ansel and Tamsin are thrown together running a fundraiser booth. Old ease resurfaces—shared jokes, finished sentences—until a neighbor mentions how broken Tamsin was after that summer. Beat: warmth interrupted by accountability.

chapters.title: June's Doubt
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. June confides she isn't sure she wants the wedding her family bought. Ansel, hired to sell the dream, tells her the truth: a wedding can't manufacture belonging. Beat: Ansel's belief system inverted by their own client.

chapters.title: The Ledger
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Ansel hands over the ledger evidence. Tamsin reads the family name and understands Ansel's departure was flight, not indifference—but understanding isn't forgiveness. Beat: the letter's question answered at last, eleven years too late and somehow on time.

chapters.title: Halloran Makes an Offer
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. The developer offers Ansel a permanent contract—buying their silence about the ledger—in exchange for making the wedding his showcase. Ansel stalls, terrified of losing the only work they trust. Beat: temptation framed as security.

chapters.title: Low Tide
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Tamsin and Ansel walk the exposed flats at low tide, and Tamsin asks the real question: not why did you leave, but why couldn't you tell me you were scared. Ansel has no polished answer. Beat: raw honesty without resolution; the closest they've been in a decade.

chapters.title: The Hearing
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. At the county hearing on the dock, Ansel testifies despite the developer's threats; the islanders rally, and the claim collapses on procedural grounds—justice won outside any courtroom romance. Beat: public courage; private cost looming.

chapters.title: Everything I Planned
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. Fired and blacklisted by Halloran's network, Ansel packs to leave before the wedding, planning to send the confession instead of speaking it. Priya catches them packing and calls it cowardice with good stationery. Beat: rock bottom; the pattern named.

chapters.title: Last Ferry of the Season
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Tamsin preps the final crossing, telling herself she's done waiting. She sees Ansel running down the pier through fog, missing the boat by seconds—and holds the line longer than schedule allows. Beat: hope as a deliberate act.

chapters.title: The Sentence
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. On the deck of the last ferry, in front of strangers and gulls, Ansel finally says it aloud: I left because staying meant admitting I was loved, and I didn't believe I could keep it. No music, no lighting design. Beat: climax; the decade-long rehearsal performed unrehearsed.

chapters.title: Open Water
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Tamsin doesn't answer with absolution; she answers with a ticket stub and a seat beside her. They talk the whole crossing—not promises, but terms. Beat: earned tenderness; love as a decision renewed daily.

chapters.title: A Wedding, Off the Books
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV, epilogue. Spring: June and Priya marry small on the rebuilt dock, planned free by Ansel, ferried by Tamsin. Ansel still trains the muscle daily—but now the exercise is staying. Final beat: inheritance reclaimed, belonging chosen, the sentence retired.
